Nov 18, 2026

Automatically retrieve SAML IdP signing certificates

Cloudflare OneAccess

Cloudflare Access can retrieve signing certificates from a SAML identity provider's metadata endpoint. Your IdP can publish replacement certificates without requiring you to upload each one to Access.

In your generic SAML identity provider configuration, set Signing certificate source to Fetch certificates from IdP metadata and enter the IdP metadata URL. The endpoint must return SAML metadata XML over public HTTPS, without authentication or redirects. It must not return a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS).

For API configurations, use metadata_url instead of manual certificate fields:

Access caches the certificates and does not poll the endpoint.

Removing a compromised certificate from metadata does not immediately revoke the cached certificate or existing Access sessions. For setup, planned rotation, and emergency replacement guidance, refer to Discover IdP signing certificates.

Nov 11, 2026

GitHub automatically detects leaked Access service tokens

AccessCloudflare One

GitHub secret scanning automatically detects Cloudflare Access service token secrets exposed in public repositories and reports them to Cloudflare. Access then disables the affected token and emails account administrators.

Other secret scanning tools can identify Access service tokens using their consistent Client Secret format: cfast_, followed by 40 alphanumeric characters and an eight-character hexadecimal checksum. For tools that support custom detection rules, use this regular expression to find possible secrets:

This pattern applies to Client Secrets created on or after August 26, 2026, not legacy 64-character hexadecimal secrets. Matching the pattern does not validate the checksum or confirm that the secret is active. For details, refer to Client Secret format.

Recover a leaked service token

Before you can re-enable a leaked token, you must rotate its secret.

Leaked secrets do not support a rotation grace period. When you rotate one, the previous secret is discarded immediately. Update your services with the new secret, then re-enable the token.

For API rotations, omit previous_client_secret_expires_at. A future expiration returns 400. Attempting to re-enable the token before rotation returns 409.

For recovery steps and leak metadata fields, refer to Recover a leaked service token.

Nov 6, 2026

Sign in to Cloudflare Access with passkeys

AccessCloudflare One

Cloudflare Access supports passkeys as a login method for protected applications and the App Launcher. Users can sign in with a passkey saved on their device, security key, or password manager instead of entering a one-time PIN or configuring an identity provider.

Users verify their identity with an existing login method once before enrolling a passkey. Administrators choose which applications accept passkeys and can remove a user's registered passkeys. Access policies still determine whether a user can access an application.

For setup and enrollment instructions, refer to Passkeys.

Nov 2, 2026

Organize and authorize Access service tokens with tags

Cloudflare OneAccess

You can now assign key-value tags to Access service tokens and use those tags to organize credentials or control application access. Each token supports up to five tags, such as environment: production or team: payments.

Add or edit tags when you create or update a token in the dashboard or service token API. You can search and filter by tag on the Service Tokens page. Tags also appear in Resource Tagging, where you can query them alongside other tagged resources.

The Service Token Tag policy selector matches valid tokens with an exact key-value pair. Use it in a Service Auth policy to authorize tokens by environment or team without listing each token individually. For example, this API policy configuration accepts valid tokens tagged environment: production:

For setup instructions, refer to Tag service tokens and Authorize service tokens by tag.

Oct 30, 2026

Inspect provisioned users and groups with the SCIM population viewer

Cloudflare OneAccess

The SCIM population viewer lets you inspect the users and groups provisioned to Cloudflare One by each identity provider. You can check which resources Cloudflare has received without making API requests or opening a support ticket.

In Zero Trust > Integrations > Identity providers, select a user or group count in SCIM resources to open the viewer. You can:

  • Search users by username, email, name, or resource ID, and groups by name or resource ID.
  • Inspect resource attributes in formatted or JSON views.
  • View group members and compare Cloudflare and IdP resource IDs with provisioning logs.
  • Delete individual resources from the Cloudflare SCIM population when you have edit permission.

The viewer shows provisioned resources rather than provisioning event history. Use SCIM provisioning logs to investigate failed requests. Existing SCIM deprovisioning and policy behavior remain unchanged.

For dashboard instructions and API examples, refer to View SCIM users and groups.

Oct 28, 2026

Google Workspace SCIM user provisioning through generic SAML

AccessCloudflare One

System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) is an open standard that synchronizes user identities between an identity provider and a service. For more information, refer to SCIM provisioning. Google Workspace is rolling out custom SCIM profiles in beta. Organizations with access to the feature can use Google's built-in provisioning service to send user updates and deprovisioning events to Cloudflare One.

You must use a generic SAML identity provider in Cloudflare One. The dedicated Google Workspace integration does not support SCIM. Configure a SAML app in Google, then enter the Cloudflare SCIM endpoint and secret in the app's autoprovisioning settings. Turn on Enable user deprovisioning in Cloudflare One to revoke active Access sessions when Google deprovisions a user. Google's configured deprovisioning delay still applies. Support for the existing Google Workspace OIDC client will be added once Google adds support for OIDC + SCIM.

Group membership is configured separately. Have the Google SAML app send a groups attribute to include the user's selected Google groups during authentication. Selecting groups as a SCIM provisioning scope does not synchronize group membership, Google is still adding support for this in their SCIM provider.

Cloudflare One users must first authenticate to Access or register a device with the Cloudflare One Client before SCIM updates can apply. Availability of custom SCIM profiles depends on Google's beta rollout.

For setup instructions, refer to Google Workspace (SAML/SCIM).

Oct 28, 2026

Filter MCP tool-call analytics by response status

AccessCloudflare One

MCP tool-call analytics support a response_status query parameter on the account, portal, and server timeseries endpoints. Use success, error, or cached to count one status, or all to include every status.

The default is success. Previously, counts included failed and cached calls. If you need the previous all-status counts, set response_status=all explicitly:

The response includes the selected response_status. Invalid values, including an empty value, return 400.

For all query parameters and scoped endpoints, refer to View tool-call analytics.

Oct 27, 2026

Fully customize user-facing Access pages

Cloudflare OneAccess

Cloudflare Access now supports HTML and Liquid templates for login, identity-denied, forbidden, and command-line approval pages. Custom templates allow you to control the branding and appearance of each supported page. Liquid variables allow you to provide custom instructions to users or provide a clear reason why they were blocked.

Create templates in the Cloudflare One dashboard, validate them in the editor, and assign them to applications or set account defaults.

Custom templates are available on Zero Trust Pay-as-you-go and Enterprise plans. They are not available on the Zero Trust Free plan.

For supported page types, template examples, and setup instructions, refer to Access custom pages.

Oct 14, 2026

Account context in Access deny redirects

AccessCloudflare One

App-aware Cloudflare Access deny redirects include an account_id query parameter when account context is available. Custom block pages can use it to identify the account that owns the application represented by kid.

For example, a custom redirect can include:

The account ID helps block-page integrations look up applications through account-scoped APIs. It is context, not proof of authentication or authorization.

For parameter descriptions and an example, refer to Custom redirect URL parameters.

Oct 14, 2026

Infrastructure applications support a configurable session duration

Cloudflare OneAccess

Infrastructure applications now have a configurable session duration with a default value of 24 hours. You can set the session duration when creating or editing an infrastructure application in the dashboard or via the API.

When the session duration elapses, any active SSH connections through that application will be closed, and users will need to reconnect. Previously, infrastructure applications did not enforce a session duration limit. Sessions could persist beyond 24 hours in some cases, but were never guaranteed beyond 10 hours due to Gateway connection limits.

When a target matches multiple infrastructure applications, the shortest session duration applies.

For more information, refer to Session duration.

Oct 2, 2026

New strict service token authentication setting for Access

AccessCloudflare One

The strict service token authentication setting applies consistent behavior to requests made with service tokens. When the setting is on for a Zero Trust organization, Access handles requests with service token headers as follows:

  • If authentication or authorization fails, Access always returns 401 or 403 instead of redirecting the client to the login page with 302.
  • Only Service Auth policies can authorize the request. Access ignores Allow policies and any CF_Authorization cookie sent with the request.
  • Access does not return a CF_Authorization cookie to the client after successful authentication. Subsequent requests should continue to use service token headers.
  • Failed requests for recognized service tokens appear in Access authentication logs.

Zero Trust organizations created on or after October 5, 2026 have strict service token authentication turned on by default and cannot turn it off. Cloudflare recommends that existing organizations turn it on as well.

Organizations created before October 5, 2026 can configure the setting in the dashboard or through the API.

  1. In the Cloudflare dashboard ↗︎, go to Zero Trust > Access controls > Access settings.

    Go to Access settings ↗

  2. Under Manage service tokens, turn on Strict service token authentication.

  3. In the confirmation dialog, select Enable.

To turn off strict service token authentication, turn off the setting and select Disable.

To turn off strict service token authentication, set strict_service_token_auth to false.

For behavior and configuration details, refer to Strict service token authentication.

Oct 1, 2026

Simplified permissions for tagging targets with Access for Infrastructure

Cloudflare OneAccess

You can now tag targets using only the Zero Trust Write API token permission. Previously, tagging targets through the API required both Zero Trust Write and Tag Write permissions on the API token.

This change applies to inline target tagging through the Infrastructure Access Targets API. Tagging resources through the general Resource Tagging API still requires the Tag Admin, Tag Write, or equivalent role.

For more information, refer to Tag targets.

Sep 24, 2026

MCP server portals are now generally available

AccessCloudflare One

MCP server portals are now generally available to all Cloudflare customers. A portal gives users one endpoint for approved Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Cloudflare Access logs tool, prompt, and resource activity.

Since the open beta, MCP server portals have added:

  • Gateway routing for HTTP logging and data loss prevention (DLP) scanning
  • Code Mode policies that control how portals reduce tool definitions and token use
  • Static OAuth client credentials for providers that do not support Dynamic Client Registration
  • Session management for reconnecting servers and changing authorizations from the portal
  • Service token authentication for autonomous agents and machine-to-machine access
  • Logpush support for exporting portal activity to external storage or a security information and event management (SIEM) system

To create a portal and connect an MCP client, refer to MCP server portals.

Sep 23, 2026

Authentication options for Google Workspace identity providers

Access

Google Workspace identity provider integrations now include prompt controls and device-scoped login hints in the Cloudflare dashboard and API.

Choose Google's default behavior, silent authentication, consent, or account selection. If silent authentication cannot use an active Google session, Access retries once with Google's default interactive flow.

Access can also send a domain-matched login hint. It sends the hint when one email from a previous Access login on the same device matches the Google Workspace domain.

For configuration details, refer to Google Workspace authentication options.

Sep 22, 2026

Automatically manage inactive Access service tokens

Access

Cloudflare Access administrators can now automatically disable or delete inactive service tokens. Administrators can set an inactivity period from 30 to 365 days and choose what Access does when a token reaches that limit.

To be eligible for cleanup, a token must be older than the configured period, must not have successfully authenticated during that period, and must not be directly referenced by an Access policy rule. Cleanup runs gradually in the background, so eligible tokens may not be disabled or deleted immediately.

For configuration instructions, refer to Manage inactive service tokens.

Sep 22, 2026

Private MCP server support for MCP server portals

Cloudflare OneAccess

MCP server portals can now connect to MCP servers available only on your private network. The portal uses Cloudflare Gateway to reach private hostnames and IP addresses without exposing the MCP server to the public Internet.

Connect the server network to Cloudflare with Cloudflare Tunnel, Cloudflare Mesh, or another Cloudflare One connector. Configure a private hostname or CIDR route, then turn on Route traffic through Cloudflare Gateway when you add the server. OAuth authorization server endpoints, such as the authorization and token endpoints, must be accessible on the public Internet. If Cloudflare automatically registers the OAuth client through Dynamic Client Registration (DCR), the registration endpoint must also be accessible on the public Internet.

For setup instructions, refer to Connect a private MCP server.

Sep 15, 2026

Access for Infrastructure now supports tagged targets and tag-based target criteria

Cloudflare OneAccess

Access for Infrastructure now integrates with Resource Tagging. You can attach key-value tags to infrastructure targets and use them in access policies.

You can manage tags on targets inline when you create or edit a target or through the central Resource Tagging API. Cloudflare keeps tags in sync across both methods.

Infrastructure applications also support a target criteria model with include, require, and exclude operators. Each operator can match targets by hostname, tag, or both.

  • Include matches targets that have any of the specified values.
  • Require matches targets that have all of the specified values.
  • Exclude rejects targets that have any of the specified values.

For more information, refer to Add an infrastructure application.

Sep 14, 2026

Require fresh authentication for SAML identity providers

Access

Cloudflare Access can now request fresh authentication from a SAML identity provider for every login. Turn on Require reauthentication in the Cloudflare dashboard, or set force_authn to true through the API. Access will then set ForceAuthn to true in signed and unsigned SAML authentication requests.

This option is useful when an application requires users to reauthenticate at the identity provider instead of relying on an existing identity provider session. The default value is false.

For configuration details, refer to Require fresh authentication at the identity provider.

Aug 26, 2026

Access service token secrets use a scannable format

Access

Cloudflare Access service token Client Secrets created on or after August 26, 2026, use the format cfast_[40 alphanumeric characters][8-character checksum]. The prefix and checksum make these credentials easier for secret scanning tools to identify with fewer false positives.

Existing service token secrets continue to work and do not require rotation. Both formats use the same Client ID and the same CF-Access-Client-Id and CF-Access-Client-Secret authentication headers.

For more information, refer to Service tokens.

Aug 25, 2026

Grace periods for service token rotation

Access

Cloudflare Access administrators can now choose a grace period when rotating a service token secret. Both secrets remain valid during the grace period, giving administrators time to update services without interrupting authentication.

The dashboard offers grace periods from one hour to 30 days. Administrators can also revoke the previous secret immediately. The API accepts an RFC 3339 expiration time for custom rotation schedules.

For configuration instructions, refer to Rotate service token secrets.

Aug 25, 2026

Temporarily turn off Access service tokens

Access

Cloudflare Access administrators can now temporarily turn off service tokens without deleting them. A disabled token cannot authenticate, but its configuration remains available so administrators can turn it on again later.

Turning off a token also stops any previous secret in an active rotation grace period. Use this control to contain suspected credential exposure or pause an automated service.

For configuration instructions, refer to Turn a service token on or off.

Aug 25, 2026

MCP server portals support MCP 2026-07-28 specification

Cloudflare OneAccess

MCP server portals support the stateless MCP 2026-07-28 specification for client and upstream server connections.

The portal's /mcp endpoint automatically accepts stateless MCP 2026-07-28 requests and earlier 2025 Streamable HTTP clients. When the portal connects to an upstream Streamable HTTP server, it checks for MCP 2026-07-28 support and falls back to the 2025 handshake when needed. Client and upstream protocol selection are independent, so clients and servers can upgrade separately without portal configuration changes.

SSE connections continue to use the legacy protocol. For details, refer to MCP server portal transport and protocol compatibility.

Aug 19, 2026

Access resource lists now support resource-scoped roles

AccessCloudflare Fundamentals

Members with only resource-scoped Access roles can now open Access resource list pages in the Cloudflare dashboard and call list endpoints in the API. They no longer need an additional account-scoped read-only role to list resources.

The dashboard and API return only resources included in the member's permission policy scopes. Filtering applies to Access applications, policies, service tokens, and identity providers. This allows administrators to delegate specific Access resources without granting account-wide visibility. Previously, the dashboard blocked these list pages and API list requests returned 403 responses.

For members with the Cloudflare Access App Admin role, policy lists include policies attached directly to the selected application. Reusable policies appear only when the member has the Cloudflare Access Policy Admin role for those policies.

For role definitions and assignment details, refer to Resource-scoped roles and Role scopes.

Aug 14, 2026

You can now enable Access on a Worker or all Workers at once

WorkersAccess

You now have two new ways to protect your Workers with Cloudflare Access.

Protect an application across all its domains at once

Until now, if a Worker was reachable on a route, a Custom Domain, and a workers.dev URL, you had to manually add each one to an Access application and keep the list in sync whenever routes or domains changed.

Now, Access attaches the policy to the Worker itself, so every associated domain and preview URL stays protected even when its routes or domains change.

Protect all new and existing Workers by default

Make all Workers private by default, so every existing and newly created Worker requires sign-in before anyone can reach it.

If a specific Worker should remain publicly accessible, add a Worker-level bypass to exempt it.

Whether you protect a single application or all Workers at once, you can choose whether to protect preview deployments only or both previews and production, and control who can sign in by Cloudflare account membership, email address, or email domain.

For more advanced policy options, edit the policy in Zero Trust ↗︎.

View all of your Worker Access policies

You can view and manage all of your Access policies in the Access tab of the Workers & Pages section in the dashboard.

See who is accessing your Worker

When Access is enabled on your Worker, every authenticated request includes ctx.access. Call ctx.access.getIdentity() to get the user's email, name, and groups — no manual JWT validation required.

Test Access locally

You can now test Cloudflare Access locally with wrangler dev. Add a dev block to your wrangler.jsonc:

Your Worker will receive this identity through ctx.access and ctx.access.getIdentity(), letting you test authenticated and unauthenticated flows without deploying. Remove the dev block to simulate unauthenticated requests.

API and programmatic access

You can also set up these policies through the Workers API instead of the dashboard.

Aug 12, 2026

Independent MFA supports FIDO2 for infrastructure applications

Cloudflare OneAccess

Infrastructure applications support independent multi-factor authentication (MFA) with FIDO2 keys. You can allow ssh_fido2_key, piv_key, or both in application-level and policy-level MFA settings.

Users enroll FIDO2 keys through the App Launcher and connect with the generated SSH identity. FIDO2 keys for SSH are separate from browser-based WebAuthn security keys and Personal Identity Verification (PIV) keys.

For setup instructions, refer to Enroll a FIDO2 key for infrastructure apps and Configure MFA for infrastructure applications.
